prize_parts.citation: for the invention and realisation of optical lattice clocks, whose magic-wavelength trapping of neutral atoms brought frequency measurement to the 10^-18 level

statement.case_for: Optical lattice clocks combine a clean, identifiable idea (Katori's magic-wavelength lattice, which removes the trap-induced shift of the clock transition) with an unambiguous experimental outcome: fractional uncertainties near 1e-18, a performance that now exceeds the caesium definition of the second. Ye's work took the scheme to record accuracy and stability and used it for relativistic redshift measurements over millimetre scales, clock comparisons and searches for variation of constants. The credit boundary is the cleanest on the shortlist, since two names cover proposal-and-first-realisation and record performance, and the work has been reproduced independently with Sr, Yb and other species in several countries. The redefinition of the second is still pending, so recognition is timely rather than late. I weigh this heavily because progress in physics is bounded by what we can measure and how accurately, and this is a step change in that capability that is already producing new physics tests rather than only promising them.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is that precision spectroscopy and optical frequency metrology were recognised in 2005 (the comb and laser-based precision spectroscopy) and ion control and ion clocks in 2012, so the committee may see lattice clocks as an incremental continuation of an already honoured line rather than a new discovery. A second concern is that the prize would honour a measurement instrument, whose most striking consequences (redefinition of the second, geodesy, constant-variation limits) are still prospective, and ion-clock groups and other lattice-clock teams (for example Lemonde, Ludlow and the Al+ line) lie outside the two credited names. My reading is that the magic-wavelength concept is a distinct invention from the comb and from ion trapping, but I recognise this is a judgement and not a settled fact. I am also relying on my own recollection of the priority history rather than on verified documentation.

responses.point: Mehlig ranks the Kane-Mele-Molenkamp topological insulator candidate first because it reorganised how condensed-matter phases are classified, with a topological invariant rather than a broken symmetry, and notes that Molenkamp's HgTe observation followed the uncredited Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang proposal.
responses.response: I accept the conceptual depth, and several colleagues rank B047 highly, so I do not dismiss it. But this is the candidate furthest from my expertise and I will not pretend to adjudicate the priority question between Kane and Mele, the Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang HgTe proposal and Hasan's three-dimensional work. That the credit dispute is shared by Danielsson, Eriksson, Johansson, Lindroth and you suggests it is genuinely unresolved, and a three-name cap leaves out Zhang, who cannot be honoured, and Hasan. The 2016 prize on topological phases also leaves some risk of overlap, as you and Olsson both note. I would not oppose B047 on merit, but I think B010 is the safer attribution, and I would like to hear how you propose to settle the experimental slot between Molenkamp and Hasan.

responses.point: Lindroth ranks optical lattice clocks first alongside me and asks whether the lattice-clock concept should be separated from the later ion and Al+ clock lines, and how to weigh Katori's proposal against Ye's accuracy milestones.
responses.response: I agree on the core case and want to take the separation question seriously. I would draw the line at the magic-wavelength trapping scheme: that is what Katori proposed and what Ye drove to its present accuracy, so the citation should be framed around lattice clocks and not around optical clocks generally. This keeps ion clocks (which sit near the 2012 territory) outside the citation without denigrating them. On the relative weight of the two, I do not think the committee needs to rank them, because the two-name configuration is stable under either reading. Where I would press back gently is on 'timely': the redefinition of the second has not happened, so I would not lean on it in the citation.

responses.point: Johansson ranks circuit QED first, describes it as the architecture of most superconducting processors, and openly flags both his proximity to the field and the question of returning to superconducting circuits so soon after 2025, while noting that Girvin and Huang are not credited.
responses.response: I appreciate the candour about proximity, and I agree circuit QED is enormously consequential; I ranked it fourth and would credit the experimentalists Schoelkopf and Wallraff, with Blais a defensible third. My disagreement is about timing and attribution. A prize to Clarke, Devoret and Martinis for circuits was awarded only last year, and the 2004 theory proposal has five authors, so a three-name cap forces an arbitrary cut among Blais, Girvin and Huang. Lattice clocks have no comparable recent overlap and a cleaner two-name boundary. I would keep B041 on the list as a strong later candidate rather than treat it as the first choice this year.

responses.point: Danielsson places twisted bilayer graphene first because it is a concrete, original discovery that gave a widely adopted platform, with a natural theory-plus-experiment trio, while acknowledging that the pairing mechanism is still debated and credit boundaries are not clean.
responses.response: I agree with the structure of the argument (prediction by Bistritzer and MacDonald, discovery by Jarillo-Herrero) and ranked B051 fifth, so I am not hostile to it. My reservation is the one you partly raise: the superconductivity mechanism is unsettled, the experimental first author and other moire platform groups are outside the credited names, and the understanding is younger than the observation. Optical lattice clocks have a stable interpretation and independent confirmation in many laboratories, which for me puts maturity and attribution in their favour. If the committee wants a condensed-matter prize this year I would support B051 as my second alternative to B046, but I would not place it above a clock prize.

uncertainties: Whether the committee regards lattice clocks as sufficiently distinct from the 2005 comb and 2012 ion-control prizes, or as a continuation of the same story.
Whether ion-clock and other lattice-clock groups (outside the credited names) require a wider configuration than the two supplied names permit.
My recollection of the priority history of the magic-wavelength proposal has not been independently verified from the supplied material.
Whether a prize centred on a measurement capability is weighed less than a discovery of new phenomena, given that the redefinition of the second has not yet happened.
statement.conflict_note: I should flag that my doctoral period included a research stay in John Hall's laboratory in Boulder; Hall shared the 2005 prize for precision spectroscopy and comb techniques, which is adjacent to, but not part of, the B010 credit, and Jun Ye is associated with that environment, so the committee should judge whether this connection requires recusal on B010. I also work in atomic physics and quantum optics at Lund, and I have European quantum-memory collaborations and a quantum-technology programme role (WACQT), which could touch the quantum-information candidates (B046, B041, B058) in a general way. No specific personal relationship with Katori, Ye, Cirac or Zoller is apparent from the provided profile.
